newsitem.title: CHINA: China telecom operators cut mobile phone prices.
newsitem.headline: China telecom operators cut mobile phone prices.

text.p: China's telecommunications operators have cut their mobile phone prices in major cities as competition to win market share heats up, company officials said on Tuesday.
"Price cuts have been carried out in all major cities," an official with the Beijing unit of the China United Telecommunication Corp (China Unicom) told Reuters.
China Unicom is the newcomer in the nation's telecommunications sector, competing with the more established Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications (MPT), which once had a monopoly.

China Unicom has announced deep cuts on its mobile phone prices since the start of this year in major cities, including Beijing, Shanghai and Chengdu, the capital of the southwestern province of Sichuan.
"We have to be 400-1,000 yuan cheaper than China Telecom," the official said in a reference to the commercial arm of the MPT. "Otherwise, we would have no competitive edge."
Unicom has focused on mobile telephone operations so far and now has 150,000 mobile phone customers nationwide and 30,000 in Beijing alone, the official said.
There are about 240,000 mobile telephone users overall in Beijing.
The Unicom official said the reductions in Beijing were a response to cuts by the Beijing Wireless Communications Bureau, the local arm of the MPT.
The Beijing bureau has trimmed its mobile phone prices four times since the start of this year, a bureau official said.
The price cuts were aimed at cementing the company's position as the market leader, she said.
Ericsson phones have been cut to 7,300-7,500 yuan ($879-$903) from over 11,000 yuan at the start of the year, she said. The prices include network connection fees.

The price of the most expensive phone, a Motorola, had been cut to 16,910 yuan from 21,000 yuan at the beginning of this year, she said. The cheapest mobile phone, a Philips, was now 4,980 yuan, she said without giving a previous price.

Mobile phone operators have recently expanded their networks to Beijing's underground railway, enabling customers to make and receive calls while travelling on the system, the Economic Information Daily said.
